cases.answer: In the retrospective HFpEF SGLT2i cohort, the benefits on ΔGLS, ΔE/e', ΔLAVI, ΔNT-proBNP and ΔPIIINP were seen in both diabetic and non-diabetic subgroups (all P < 0.001 within subgroup). No significant interaction between SGLT2i treatment and diabetes status was found for any outcome (all P for interaction > 0.05, Table 6). The authors read this as showing the effects are independent of glycemic control. That is an inference from a non-significant subgroup interaction. The article reports no direct adjustment for, or analysis of, changes in glycemic measures such as HbA1c, so the interaction test alone does not strictly establish independence from glycemic changes. The non-diabetic subgroup showed similar changes (e.g., ΔGLS −2.45 vs −0.26), which is consistent with the authors' claim.

cases.answer: In Gao's external validation cohort (n = 288), the CCTA-based nomogram had an AUC of 0.932 and good calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow P = 0.382). Its AUC was significantly higher than that of every individual predictor there. The authors say recalibration may be needed in lower-risk outpatient settings. The external cohort was higher-risk: its MACE rate was 31.6% versus 16.4% in the derivation cohort, it had more comorbidities, and it came from tertiary referral centers. The model was validated only in that higher-risk population, so calibration in lower-risk outpatients is untested.

cases.answer: In Ying Sun's study, the CV score (the CHA2DS2-VASc-based score) was not an independent predictor of no-reflow in men. Among male patients the only independent predictor was platelet count, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.993 (95% CI 0.987–0.999, p = 0.033). An AOR below 1 means higher platelet count was associated with lower odds of no-reflow.

cases.answer: The universal-control claim is stated only in the abstract (and a discussion sentence with an exception), and the results text contradicts it. The abstract says all spironolactone patients were controlled at BP below 130/80 mmHg after 1 month, but the mean post-treatment office BP was 125 ± 11/72 ± 8 mmHg. The results section says one of nine spironolactone participants did not reach the target office BP, with 140/67 mmHg at 1 month. That target was defined there as <140/90. The discussion says all reached the 130/80 target 'with the exception' of one patient who reached the diastolic but not the systolic target. So the universal claim is not supported by the individual-level results. The supporting data are only group means, and the trial was small (n = 9 spironolactone, n = 8 control) and single blinded. Self-measured BP target (<135/85) was reached by all in the spironolactone group.

cases.answer: Efficacy inputs came from the DELIVER trial for dapagliflozin and from a pooled analysis of PARAGLIDE-HF and PARAGON-HF for sacubitril–valsartan. The abstract says costs were based on 2022 US prices. The Methods say drug costs were 75% of the US National Average Drug Acquisition Cost (NADAC) extracted in July 2023, so the price basis is described slightly differently in the two places. Annual costs were $4,951.57 for dapagliflozin and $5,576.06 for sacubitril–valsartan. For the composite outcome (total HF hospitalizations plus cardiovascular death), the CNT was $148,547.13 (95% CI $103,982.99–306,997.39) for dapagliflozin and $245,346.77 (95% CI $139,401.58–1,734,155.60) for sacubitril–valsartan. For all-cause mortality the CNTs were $1,128,958.15 (CI $401,077.24–∞) for dapagliflozin and $2,185,816.71 (CI $607,790.87–∞) for sacubitril–valsartan.
